ai_peak.text: This metric suggests AI is still in the acceleration phase, roughly 340 days before a potential peak. Caveat: analogies to past bubbles often break down due to structural differences in technology, capital, and market dynamics.

buffett.text: Market cap to GDP suggests AI valuations are following the dot-com trajectory but at an accelerated pace, currently at late-1998 intensity levels. A skeptical reader should note that analogies based on single metrics can mislead, since AI companies have real revenue streams unlike many dot-com firms.

capex.text: AI infrastructure spending mirrors the dot-com era's escalating capex cycle, suggesting sustained investment momentum ahead. Caveat: infrastructure buildout may prove more rational than dot-com spending, justifying higher absolute levels and different trajectory.

ipo_froth.text: IPO enthusiasm shows similar early-stage dynamics to the dot-com boom, with first-day pops still modest relative to peak froth. The pattern suggests room for further euphoria before any potential reversal. Caveat: IPO metrics lag actual market peaks, so this analogy may understate how far sentiment has already advanced.

it_invest.text:
IT investment share shows AI spending already matching dot-com peak intensity, suggesting the sector has reached a critical valuation threshold. The analogy implies continued investment momentum through late 2026, though sector concentration may mask whether gains reflect genuine productivity or speculative excess.

Caveat: Historical analogies assume similar institutional behavior, but AI's utility in cost reduction and revenue generation may justify higher sustained investment than dot-com ever achieved.

margin_debt.text: Margin debt has roughly doubled since ChatGPT, reaching 41% of dot-com peak intensity. The pattern of rising leverage mirrors the late-1990s acceleration phase, suggesting investors are increasingly confident or complacent. Keep in mind that regulatory changes and circuit breakers since 2000 may prevent debt from reaching comparable extremes.

market_concentration.text: AI market concentration is rising steeply but remains well below dot-com extremes, suggesting earlier bubble stages. The compression ratio implies a faster timeline, but concentration alone cannot predict peaks, only describe current structure.

monetary.text: AI sentiment and monetary conditions are significantly cooler than dot-com's frenzied peak, suggesting the analogy breaks down here. This metric doesn't support a near-term bubble conclusion. Caveat: sentiment measures are subjective and may not capture hidden leverage or irrational deployment of capital in private markets.

nasdaq.text: The Nasdaq shows AI still in its acceleration phase, roughly where dot-com was a year before the peak. This metric alone doesn't tell us whether AI's fundamentals are sounder than dot-com's hype, only that the price trajectory looks similar so far.

price_appreciation.text: AI valuations are climbing steeply but have not yet matched dot-com's frothiest phase. The analogy suggests room for further gains before any potential peak. Caveat: past price patterns do not determine future ones, especially across different technologies and market structures.

semis.text: Semiconductor production lacks a clear peak phase in the dot-com era, making this metric unsuitable for drawing parallels. Skeptics should remember that chip demand has structural drivers today that didn't exist then, potentially invalidating any historical comparison.

sentiment.text: Consumer sentiment shows no bubble pattern in AI, remaining flat while dot-com sentiment surged toward its peak. This suggests either different investor psychology or that consumer confidence hasn't yet responded to AI hype the way it did then. Keep in mind that sentiment measures may capture institutional and retail confidence differently across eras.

sp500.text: The S&P 500's gain since ChatGPT mirrors the dot-com acceleration phase, suggesting the AI rally has room to run before peaking. However, the compression ratio of 1.23 assumes history repeats on a faster timeline, which depends heavily on whether market cycles truly accelerate or if this comparison cherry-picks convenient similarities.

speculation.text: Speculative fervor in AI is building at a pace slightly faster than the dot-com run-up, currently at about one-third the intensity seen at that market's peak. The caveat: past compression ratios offer no guarantee about when or whether AI speculation will actually peak.

tech_leadership.text: Tech leadership concentration has risen sharply since ChatGPT, tracking the dot-com pattern at a compressed pace. The analogy suggests a potential peak around late 2026, though this assumes structural similarities that may not hold. Caveat: the metric measures leadership only, not whether the underlying AI investments prove economically valuable.

tech_orders.text: Equipment orders show AI adoption accelerating at a pace similar to dot-com in 1999, though at lower absolute intensity. The analogy suggests continued growth before any potential plateau. Caveat: equipment cycles depend heavily on capex plans that can shift suddenly with policy or rates.

valuation.text: AI valuations are rising steeply but haven't reached dot-com peak intensity yet, suggesting room for further gains if the pattern holds. Caveat: different fundamentals may support higher valuations this time around.

valuation_multiple.text: Market valuations show AI stocks climbing at a pace similar to dot-com during its acceleration phase, suggesting the current enthusiasm could sustain further gains before any correction. The caveat: valuation multiples alone don't account for actual earnings growth, which differs significantly between the two eras.

yield_curve.text: The yield curve shows no signs of mimicking the dot-com era's inversion pattern that preceded the crash. The spread remains stable rather than tightening toward distress levels, suggesting different economic conditions between the two periods. Caveat: yield curve dynamics depend heavily on Federal Reserve policy, which operates under entirely different frameworks and constraints than it did in 2000.
